title: Why a sad play feels good
hookLine: a theater audience weeps at a tragedy and walks out into the night strangely at peace, and a Kashmiri teacher asks why
carry: rasa: a taste of the awareness called Shiva
tomorrow: she loves him, he's standing right there, and she feels nothing. why?

cards: On stage, a grieving lover cries out, and down in the seats people are wiping their eyes. Then the play ends, the lamps go out, and they walk home under the stars, talking quietly, somehow lighter than when they came.
Nobody died in their house tonight. They wept anyway, and it did them good. Why does a sad story feel like a gift?
A teacher in Kashmir thought hard about that question, and his answer reached all the way to Shiva. His name is Abhinavagupta.

teach.b: Abhinavagupta is remembered as a teacher who wrote about two things that might seem far apart: the art of theater and poetry, and the way to Shiva. In his tradition they turn out to be close. Start with the theater.
Indian poetics speaks of rasa, the taste of a work of art. In a tragedy there's real sorrow in the story, but it isn't your private sorrow. You don't have to fix anything or protect anyone.
So the feeling comes to you loosened from your own small worries, and you can savor it, the way you savor a flavor. That's rasa.

In that moment, Abhinavagupta explained, the viewer's little self, my problems, my plans, steps aside, and what's left is a kind of open, tasting awareness, with a quality of rest and wonder. Then he made the bold link.
If a play can briefly lift us into wide, delighted awareness, that awareness isn't something the play adds. It was there all along. And in his Shaiva teaching, that wide awareness is what Shiva is.
The theater gives a glimpse, borrowed, for an evening. The path is about seeing it without the borrowing.
Tradition adds an ending to his own story: one day he walked into a cave with his disciples, chanting, and was not seen again. Kalhana's river flowed toward calm.
Abhinavagupta's road runs through a theater, to the same quiet.

how: Students of Kashmir Shaivism and of Indian poetics read Abhinavagupta's writings with teachers, and his account of rasa is still taught to students of classical dance, music and theater.

games.q: you're in the audience. the play is sad, and you're crying, but you feel lighter, not worse. what's happening, in Abhinavagupta's account?
o: your small self has stepped aside, and you're tasting the feeling.
games.why: for him, the sorrow comes loosened from your own worries. what's left is open, tasting awareness, a glimpse of what his tradition calls Shiva.

practice: Let a little of the feeling from a song, a film or a story that once moved you return. Then gently notice what's noticing it: the feeling comes and goes, but something is aware of it the whole time, wide and quiet.
Rest there, in the tasting, without needing the feeling to stay.

wordCard.voice: Kashmir. The valley where Abhinavagupta taught that the taste of a play, the rasa, is a glimpse of the wide awareness his tradition calls Shiva. Today's word.

orig.note: rasa in Sanskrit, written in Devanagari: taste, juice, the savor of a work of art.

carryVoice: Hold on to it: rasa, a taste of the awareness called Shiva. The quiet behind every play was there all along. Same time tomorrow.
